title: Comet Tsuchinshan-ATLAS meets the ESO Supernova
caption: Comet C/2023 A3 (Tsuchinshan-ATLAS) above the ESO Supernova Planetarium, Garching, Germany
celestial: Photograph taken at the ESO Supernova Planetarium & Visitor Center, Garching bei München, Germany

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: A comet hangs in the evening sky above the ESO Supernova Planetarium & Visitor Center at ESO’s headquarters near Munich, its tail streaming upward. This is Comet C/2023 A3 (Tsuchinshan-ATLAS), photographed in October 2024.

The comet came from the Oort Cloud, a vast reservoir of icy bodies surrounding the Solar System. As it neared the Sun it warmed up and grew tails of dust and gas. It was first spotted in early 2023 by two observatories working independently, the Tsuchinshan observatory in China and an ATLAS telescope in South Africa, which is how it got its double name.

It passed closest to the Sun in September 2024 and was brightest in early October, among the brightest comets of the past two decades. It could be seen with the unaided eye, though this image stacks several exposures to bring out its faint tail.

understand.summary: A ground-based landscape photograph credited to ESO/J. C. Muñoz-Mateos. The source does not publish camera, exposure or color-processing details.
understand.eye: The comet was visible to the unaided eye, but stacking several exposures brings out more of its faint tail than the eye would see.

explore: After its pass by the Sun, the comet began the long journey back out to the edge of the Solar System. Comets from the Oort Cloud can take thousands of years or more to return, if they return at all.
alt: A comet with a long, faint tail rising from the horizon above a curved, modern building in a deep blue evening sky.
